passages.title: News of broken walls
passages.summary: Hanani reports that Jerusalem has broken walls and burned gates. Nehemiah weeps, fasts, and prays.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson studies Nehemiah’s prayer about Jerusalem. What does he ask before he speaks to the king?

contextNote.title: A public need begins within royal service
contextNote.text: Nehemiah's final words identify his position in the royal household. His prayer therefore prepares for a request to someone with power to help. He includes himself in the community's confession. Distance from Jerusalem has not removed his sense of responsibility for it.

passages.title: Permission to rebuild
passages.summary: Artaxerxes grants Nehemiah letters and wood. Nehemiah checks the walls at night before asking people to build.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Nehemiah’s answer to mockery. What preparations support his call to rebuild?

contextNote.title: A wall requires permission and resources
contextNote.text: Nehemiah asks for letters and timber before leaving the royal court. Safe travel and building materials depend on the king’s support. His prayer leads into specific requests. The wall project requires authority, work, and supplies together. The people’s local goal remains subject to a foreign ruler.

passages.title: Neighbors repair the walls
passages.summary: Priests, families, and workers repair different sections. Shallum and his daughters join the work. Some nobles refuse.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the repairs with serving God. How do named families share the work?

contextNote.title: A work list also records unequal participation
contextNote.text: The repeated names place many occupations beside one shared project. Work near homes joins public protection with household interests. The refusal of some nobles remains visible within the list. Naming workers preserves both participation and gaps in support.

passages.title: Builders keep watch
passages.summary: Sanballat and Tobiah mock the builders. Threats bring guards, weapons, and a trumpet signal to the work.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies prayer and work during threats. How do guards and the trumpet help protect workers?

contextNote.title: A long wall creates a communication problem
contextNote.text: The work spreads people across separate sections of the wall. A trumpet provides a way to gather quickly when one section faces danger. Weapons and divided tasks change the labor itself. The plan answers the practical risks created by a project too large for one household.

passages.title: Families lose land and freedom
passages.summary: Families lack food and borrow money. Some children become servants. Nehemiah orders lenders to return land and stop charges.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: What would stopping these charges change for the families?

contextNote.title: A shared building project does not remove inequality
contextNote.text: Some families lose fields and children while others lend at interest. The complaint comes from within the same community. Nehemiah must address that harm while the wall rises. External enemies are not the only threat to survival. A strong boundary cannot replace fair treatment inside it.

passages.title: Letters, threats, and a finished wall
passages.summary: Nehemiah rejects meetings and a false warning. The wall is finished in fifty-two days. Tobiah still sends threats.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Nehemiah’s response to attempts to stop him. Why does he refuse the proposed meetings?

contextNote.title: A completed wall cannot stop internal influence
contextNote.text: The ending returns to letters between Tobiah and Judah's nobles. Family connections carry influence through the barrier the builders have finished. Nehemiah's refusal to attend meetings addresses only part of that pressure. Physical defenses and social loyalties operate through different routes.

passages.title: Guards and the return register
passages.summary: Nehemiah puts Hanani and Hananiah in charge. An earlier list names returning families and their gifts.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Why do the guards need clear instructions after the wall is built?

contextNote.title: Walls do not create a populated city
contextNote.text: The account notices the difference between Jerusalem's size and its small population. Guards can protect gates, but households must also live within them. The earlier return register connects present needs with remembered families. Restoration requires people and records as well as construction.

passages.title: Ezra reads and teachers explain
passages.summary: Ezra reads God’s law to men and women. Teachers explain it. The people share food and make shelters for a feast.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies help with understanding scripture. What do the teachers do after Ezra reads?

contextNote.title: Public reading requires understanding
contextNote.text: The people gather to hear a written law. Those who teach also explain its meaning. The account links reading with understanding, grief, joy, and action. Possessing a text alone is not the same as receiving it. The community needs shared work to turn words into a way of life.

passages.title: A prayer remembers mercy and failure
passages.summary: The people fast and confess. Their prayer recalls Abraham, Egypt, the wilderness, and repeated rescue after sin.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: The people recall mercy during repeated failure. How does this shape their new promises?

contextNote.title: A prayer of rescue ends with continued dependence
contextNote.text: The long prayer recalls repeated deliverance before naming the community's present condition. They live on their land while foreign kings take its produce. Return has therefore not restored control over their work. The prayer ends with a written agreement in response to this distress.

passages.title: Promises to support worship
passages.summary: Leaders seal a written promise. Families agree to keep God’s law, rest on the Sabbath, and supply the temple.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary overview studies promises about marriage and Sabbath rest. What supplies do the families also promise?

contextNote.title: A promise must supply recurring needs
contextNote.text: The written agreement names wood, produce, money, and the workers who need support. Temple service cannot continue through one large celebration alone. The promise turns shared identity into repeated duties. Its later failures in chapter 13 test whether those duties survive ordinary life.

passages.title: Families move into Jerusalem
passages.summary: One family in ten is chosen to live in Jerusalem. Volunteers also move there. The list names workers and nearby towns.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: Who keeps daily temple service possible while families settle in different towns?

contextNote.title: Restoration changes where households live
contextNote.text: Moving families into Jerusalem addresses the gap between finished walls and a small population. The account distinguishes selection by lot from volunteering. Names and jobs show what a functioning city needs. A community's plan can also change a family's home and daily work.

passages.title: Singers celebrate the rebuilt walls
passages.summary: Priests and Levites gather for the wall’s dedication. Two groups sing along the walls. Women and children join the joy.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: How do the women and children join the public thanks?

contextNote.title: A public celebration rests on maintained labor
contextNote.text: The two groups of singers make the rebuilt walls part of a shared ceremony. Women and children also participate in its joy. The account then turns to storing supplies for temple workers. Celebration and regular support belong to the same restored life.

passages.title: Nehemiah returns and changes the rules
passages.summary: Nehemiah removes Tobiah’s goods, restores temple gifts, and closes the gates on the Sabbath. He confronts marriages with foreign women.
passages.uncertainty: Town markers show named places. The city’s gates and individual wall sections are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary overview emphasizes Sabbath rest and keeping promises to God. How do Nehemiah’s actions affect workers and families?

contextNote.title: Reform reveals what earlier promises failed to sustain
contextNote.text: The workers have returned to their fields because their support stopped. Nehemiah's interventions answer failures of the earlier written agreement. His repeated requests for remembrance also make his own role prominent. Read his forceful actions beside the needs and households they affect.
